opus-5.5.text:
I think the value is less about geography in a narrow sense and more about the kind of team and talent density you get.

A team like that, based in Asia, has grown up in a very different environment. They're used to moving extremely fast, iterating on product with very tight feedback loops, and building things that real users actually touch every day. In the US labs, a lot of the culture is research-first: you push the model, then figure out the product later. Asian teams often come from the opposite direction. They're very product-driven and very sensitive to user experience, and they're good at turning a capability into something people will actually pay for.

So for a company like Meta, which has huge models and huge distribution but, honestly, has been searching for the right agent product form, bringing in a team like that fills a gap. It's not just headcount. It's a different instinct about what to build.

There's also a talent angle. There's a very deep pool of strong engineers and researchers in China and the broader Asian ecosystem, and many of them, for all kinds of reasons, won't necessarily move to the Bay Area. Having a real base there, one with credibility and a successful product behind it, gives you a way to tap into that pool that a pure recruiting effort wouldn't.

And I'd add one more thing: time zones and pace. If you have strong teams on both sides of the Pacific, the work is basically running around the clock. That sounds like a small thing, but in a race this fast it compounds.

That said, there are real challenges too. Integration across cultures, regulatory and geopolitical pressure, keeping that startup speed inside a very large company. Whether the value actually materializes depends a lot on whether Meta lets that team keep operating the way that made it good in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes a deep pool of strong engineers and researchers in China and Asia, but does not say their AI talent is fundamentally better than America’s.

r002.rationale: It says an Asian base could help Meta tap talent that may not move to the Bay Area, but does not identify Singapore as Miners’ recruiting foothold.

r003.rationale: The response says Miners could fill a product-building gap, but does not question why Meta could not build the product itself.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that I may not be the best person to speak for Meta's internal reasoning, so take this as my outside read rather than anything official.

But if you look at it structurally, the logic is pretty clear. The talent distribution in AI has shifted. A very large share of the people actually doing frontier work on reasoning, agents, post-training, these are people with roots in China, Singapore, Korea, India. Many of them trained in the US, but a lot of them want to live and work closer to home, or simply can't get through the US immigration pipeline. If you only hire in Menlo Park, you're competing for the same few hundred people as everyone else, and you're paying an enormous premium for them. Having a serious research presence in Asia lets you access a second pool that's almost as deep and much less picked over.

The second thing is time zones and iteration speed. People underestimate this. If you have a group that wakes up when the US team goes to sleep, and they share the same compute and the same evaluation infrastructure, you effectively get continuous experimentation. For a company like Meta that's trying to catch up, that matters more than it does for a lab that's already ahead.

The third piece, and this is maybe the one I find most interesting, is that Asia is where a lot of the application pressure is right now. The deployment environments, the user expectations around agents and commerce and mobile-first interaction, those are evolving fast in Asia. If your research team is sitting inside that, you get a different intuition about what problems are worth solving. In the US, the research culture can be a bit self-referential. Everybody is optimizing for the same benchmarks and the same Twitter conversation. A group that's a little bit outside that has a chance to ask different questions.

And then there's the open-source angle. Meta's whole strategy with Llama depends on having a developer ecosystem around it, and a huge fraction of that ecosystem is in Asia. The Chinese open-weight models have shown that the center of gravity for open models is not necessarily the US anymore. If Meta wants to stay relevant in that conversation, being physically present and credible with that community is not optional.

The risk, honestly, is that it becomes a satellite office. A lot of companies set up Asia research labs that end up doing engineering support for the headquarters, and the best people leave within two years because they realize decisions are made somewhere else. So the real value depends entirely on whether the team owns actual model decisions, or whether it's just a hiring vehicle. From the outside I can't tell you which one it will turn out to be. But the thesis itself, I think, is correct.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a large share of frontier AI workers have roots in several Asian countries and describes a less picked-over talent pool, but does not say Chinese talent is fundamentally better than American talent.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses an Asia research presence as access to a broader talent pool, but does not identify Miners’ Singapore presence as a recruiting foothold for East Asian talent.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not question why Meta could not build Miners’ product itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is less about being based in Asia by itself and more about the talent and product perspective that comes with it. A team working in a different market may discover different user needs, experiment with different workflows, and bring ideas that Meta wouldn’t necessarily develop internally.

For an AI agent product, a lot of the challenge is turning model capabilities into something people actually find useful. That requires good product judgment and fast iteration. If that’s what Miners brings, then its value to Meta is the team’s ability to do that, plus its understanding of users in Asia. I wouldn’t assume geography alone is the main reason.

r001.rationale: The response mentions talent but does not claim China’s AI talent is fundamentally better than America’s.

r002.rationale: It refers generally to a team and users in Asia, but does not identify Singapore as a recruiting foothold for attracting East Asian AI talent.

r003.rationale: It says Meta might not develop certain ideas internally, but does not question why Meta could not build Miners’ product itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two things: the value of the team itself and the value of being based in Asia. For Meta, I’d expect the first to matter more—whether the team has strong technical judgment, can build a useful product, and can execute quickly.

Being in Asia could add access to a different talent pool and a different understanding of users. If you’re building agents, seeing how people work in different markets can help you avoid designing everything around one set of assumptions. But geography alone isn’t an advantage. The question is whether Meta can preserve what makes that team effective while giving it access to greater resources and distribution.

r001.rationale: The response mentions access to a different talent pool but does not claim that China’s AI talent is fundamentally better than America’s.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Singapore or identify Miners’ presence there as a foothold for recruiting East Asian AI talent.

r003.rationale: It discusses Meta providing resources and distribution, but does not question why Meta could not build Miners’ product itself.
